records.topic: What If You Fell Into a Black Hole?
records.hook: Fall into a black hole feet first. Then what?
records.openingLine: Fall into a black hole feet first. Then what?
records.secondBeat: Your feet feel far more pull than your head.
records.scientificMechanism: tidal force: the difference in gravity across a body's length, which near small black holes exceeds any material's strength
records.scenarioChange: a person falls feet first into a black hole
records.expectedConsequence: the body is stretched lengthwise and squeezed sideways; how violently depends on the black hole's mass
records.coreQuestion: If you fell into a black hole, would gravity tear you apart before you crossed the edge?
records.misconception: Bigger black holes aren't deadlier at the edge; their tidal stretch at the horizon is gentler.
visualScenes: astronaut falling feet first toward an event horizon
tidal force arrows stretching a body
diagram of four objects stretched toward a mass
Milky Way centre map with Sagittarius A* marked
event horizon size compared with Mercury's orbit
small versus giant black hole tidal comparison
editorialTitles: Why Falling Into a Giant Black Hole Is Gentler
What Spaghettification Actually Does to You

facts.claim: Spaghettification is the vertical stretching and horizontal compression of objects into long thin shapes in a very strong, non-homogeneous gravitational field.
If a person were to fall into a black hole feet first, the gravity at their feet would be much stronger than at their head, causing them to be vertically stretched.
The current best estimate of the mass of Sagittarius A* is 4.297 million solar masses.
The Schwarzschild radius of Sagittarius A* is 0.08 AU (12 million km).
Sagittarius A* lies at a distance of 26,000 light-years.

narration.text: Fall into a black hole feet first. Then what?
Your feet feel far more pull than your head.
Physicists call it spaghettification: stretched lengthwise, squeezed sideways.
Our galaxy's central black hole weighs 4.3 million Suns.
Its point of no return sits about 12 million kilometres out.
At that size, the stretch at the edge is surprisingly gentle.
Small black holes shred you long before the horizon.
So the biggest black holes let you cross intact, then never leave.

records.topic: What If the Dinosaur-Killing Asteroid Hit Today?
records.hook: One 10-kilometre asteroid ended the age of dinosaurs.
records.openingLine: One 10-kilometre asteroid ended the age of dinosaurs.
records.secondBeat: Stood on end, it would tower over Everest.
records.scientificMechanism: an impact turns the asteroid's kinetic energy into heat, shock and ejecta; fine debris and soot then block sunlight
records.scenarioChange: a Chicxulub-size asteroid strikes Earth today
records.expectedConsequence: global heating from falling debris, then years of dimmed sunlight that collapse food chains
records.coreQuestion: If the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs hit today, what would actually kill us: the crater or the sky?
records.misconception: The crater didn't kill most species; the darkened, cooled sky afterwards did.
visualScenes: asteroid beside Mount Everest for scale
Chicxulub crater map on the Yucatán coast
impact ejecta arcing around the globe
modern city skyline under darkened sky
editorialTitles: What If the Dinosaur Asteroid Hit Earth Today
Why the Sky, Not the Crater, Killed the Dinosaurs

facts.claim: The Chicxulub crater was formed slightly over 66 million years ago when an asteroid, about ten kilometers (six miles) in diameter, struck Earth.
The impactor was around 10 kilometers (6 mi) in diameter, large enough that, if set at sea level, it would have reached taller than Mount Everest.
More recent evidence suggests the crater is 300 km (190 mi) wide, and the 180 km (110 mi) ring observed is an inner wall of the larger crater.
Field research from the Hell Creek Formation shows the simultaneous mass extinction of myriad species, consistent with the impact event.

narration.text: One 10-kilometre asteroid ended the age of dinosaurs.
Stood on end, it would tower over Everest.
It struck slightly over 66 million years ago.
The crater it left is up to 300 kilometres wide.
Today, the first danger would be heat and debris raining worldwide.
Then soot and dust would dim sunlight for years.
The real killer wasn't the crater. It was the sky.

records.topic: What If Earth Had Rings Like Saturn?
records.hook: Saturn's rings cover 80 times Earth's surface area.
records.openingLine: Saturn's rings cover 80 times Earth's surface area.
records.secondBeat: Yet their total mass is surprisingly small.
records.scientificMechanism: a thin, wide ring plane reflects sunlight and casts a seasonal shadow on the planet it circles
records.scenarioChange: Earth gained a Saturn-like ring system
records.expectedConsequence: ring shadows would sweep across latitudes with the seasons, and night skies would carry a bright arc
records.coreQuestion: If Earth had rings like Saturn, would they only change the view, or the weather too?
records.misconception: Saturn's rings are enormous in area but surprisingly light, about two-thirds of Antarctica's ice.
visualScenes: Earth with a Saturn-like ring system
ring area compared with Earth's surface
night sky with a bright ring arc
editorialTitles: What If Earth Had Saturn's Rings
Why Saturn's Giant Rings Weigh So Little

facts.claim: The mass of Saturn's rings is around two-thirds the mass of the Earth's entire Antarctic ice sheet, spread across a surface area 80 times larger than that of Earth.
The Cassini Division is a 4,800-kilometre-wide (3,000 mi) region between the A Ring and B Ring.
Unlike the main rings, the E Ring is more than 2,000 km (1000 miles) thick and increases with its distance from Enceladus.
Stellar occultation revealed 13 objects, ranging from 27 meters (89') to 10 km (6 miles) across, within the F ring.

narration.text: Saturn's rings cover 80 times Earth's surface area.
Yet their total mass is surprisingly small.
All that ice weighs about two-thirds of Antarctica's ice sheet.
Gaps like the Cassini Division span 4,800 kilometres.
Give Earth rings like that, and they'd shade whole latitudes.
Seasons would shift as the shadow crossed each hemisphere.
At night, sunlit ice would arc across the sky.
So rings wouldn't just decorate Earth. They'd change its weather.

records.hook: Betelgeuse will explode, likely within 100,000 years.
records.openingLine: Betelgeuse will explode, likely within 100,000 years.
records.secondBeat: It would then shine steadily for 2 to 3 months.
records.scientificMechanism: a massive star that exhausts its fuel collapses and explodes as a supernova; its danger falls off with the square of distance
records.expectedConsequence: a brilliant new point of light for months, but at hundreds of light-years no harm to life on Earth
records.coreQuestion: If Betelgeuse exploded tonight, should Earth be worried or just look up?
records.misconception: Betelgeuse's 2019–2020 dimming wasn't the start of its explosion.
visualScenes: distance scale from Earth to Betelgeuse
brightness curve of the Great Dimming
supernova flash over a night landscape
editorialTitles: What If Betelgeuse Exploded Tonight
Why Betelgeuse's Supernova Can't Hurt Us

facts.claim: Betelgeuse is expected to end its evolution with a supernova explosion, most likely within 100,000 years.
Current best estimates put Betelgeuse at the order of 400–600 light-years from the Sun.
Starting in October 2019, Betelgeuse began to dim noticeably, and by mid-February 2020 its brightness had dropped by a factor of approximately 3, from magnitude 0.5 to 1.7.
This type of supernova would remain at roughly constant brightness for 2–3 months before rapidly dimming.

narration.text: Betelgeuse will explode, likely within 100,000 years.
It would then shine steadily for 2 to 3 months.
It sits roughly 400 to 600 light-years away.
That's far too distant to harm life on Earth.
In 2019, it dimmed by a factor of about 3.
Many wondered if the explosion had begun. It hadn't.
So the scariest star in Orion is mostly a spectacle.

records.topic: What If You Held a Teaspoon of Neutron Star?
records.hook: Why one teaspoon of neutron star would explode.
records.openingLine: Why one teaspoon of neutron star would explode.
records.scientificMechanism: neutron-star matter is held at nuclear density only by the star's own crushing gravity
records.scenarioChange: a teaspoon of neutron-star matter appeared on Earth
records.expectedConsequence: without the star's gravity to confine it, the matter would decompress explosively
records.coreQuestion: If you held a teaspoon of neutron star, what would happen first: its weight or its release?
records.misconception: A neutron-star teaspoon wouldn't just be heavy; outside the star it wouldn't stay compressed.
visualScenes: teaspoon beside the Great Pyramid for mass scale
neutron star size over a city map
editorialTitles: What a Teaspoon of Neutron Star Would Do on Earth
Why You Could Never Hold Neutron Star Matter

facts.claim: A neutron star is so dense that one teaspoon of its material would have a mass about 900 times the mass of the Great Pyramid of Giza.
Neutron stars have a radius on the order of 10 kilometers (6 miles) and a mass of about 1.4 solar masses.
The entire mass of the Earth at neutron star density would fit into a sphere 305 m in diameter.
Neutron stars are known that have rotation periods from about 1.4 ms to 30 s.

narration.text: Why one teaspoon of neutron star would explode.
It weighs about 900 Great Pyramids.
Neutron stars pack 1.4 Suns into about 10 kilometres.
Squeeze Earth that hard, and it fits in 305 metres.
Outside the star, that matter wouldn't stay compressed.
Freed from crushing gravity, it would expand violently.
So the teaspoon isn't a weight. It's a bomb.

records.hook: Yellowstone erupted 631,000 years ago. Is it overdue?
records.openingLine: Yellowstone erupted 631,000 years ago. Is it overdue?
records.secondBeat: Three caldera-forming eruptions in about 2.1 million years.
records.scientificMechanism: a large magma reservoir can empty in a caldera-forming eruption, spreading ash far downwind
records.expectedConsequence: nearby states buried in ash, continent-wide disruption to flights and crops, but not an extinction event
records.coreQuestion: If Yellowstone erupted again, would it end civilisation or just disrupt it?
records.misconception: Yellowstone isn't 'overdue'; eruptions don't run on a schedule.
visualScenes: ash fall footprint across North America
lava flow versus explosive eruption comparison
hot springs over the magma reservoir
editorialTitles: What If Yellowstone Erupted Again
Why Yellowstone Isn't Overdue

facts.claim: Volcanism began 2.15 million years ago and proceeded through three major volcanic cycles.
The climactic eruption of the first and largest cycle produced the Huckleberry Ridge Tuff about 2.08 million years ago.
The most recent supereruption, about 631,000 years ago, produced the Lava Creek Tuff and created the present Yellowstone Caldera.
Post-caldera eruptions included basalt flows, rhyolite domes and flows, with the last known magmatic eruption about 70,000 years ago.
The second cycle culminated in eruption of the Mesa Falls Tuff about 1.3 million years ago.

narration.text: Yellowstone erupted 631,000 years ago. Is it overdue?
Three caldera-forming eruptions in about 2.1 million years.
Its last magmatic eruption of any kind was 70,000 years ago.
A new supereruption would bury nearby states in ash.
Far downwind, ash would ground flights and smother crops.
But eruptions don't run on a schedule, so it isn't overdue.
Smaller lava flows are far likelier than another giant blast.
So Yellowstone's real risk is disruption, not extinction.

records.topic: What If the Atlantic Ocean Current Shut Down?
records.hook: Up to 25% of northern heat rides one current.
records.openingLine: Up to 25% of northern heat rides one current.
records.secondBeat: Climate models say it will weaken this century.
records.scientificMechanism: the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation carries warm surface water north and returns cold deep water south
records.scenarioChange: the Atlantic overturning circulation shut down
records.expectedConsequence: harsher northern European winters and shifted rain belts, arriving faster than societies usually adapt
records.coreQuestion: If the Atlantic's great current shut down, would Europe freeze, or would the real danger be speed?
records.misconception: A shutdown wouldn't plunge Europe into an ice age; a 15–20 °C crash is considered incorrect.
visualScenes: heat flow arrows toward northwest Europe
editorialTitles: What If the Atlantic Current Shut Down
Why an AMOC Collapse Isn't an Ice Age

facts.claim: The AMOC carries up to 25% of the total heat toward the northern hemisphere, and plays an important role in the climate around northwest Europe.
There is a consensus the AMOC keeps northern and western Europe warmer than it would be otherwise, with the difference of 4 °C (7.2 °F) and 10 °C (18 °F) depending on the area.
Climate models predict the AMOC will further weaken during the 21st century.
A cooling of up to 15–20 °C (27–36 °F) is generally considered incorrect.
D-O events are best known for the rapid warming of between 8 °C (15 °F) and 15 °C (27 °F) that occurred in Greenland over several decades.

narration.text: Up to 25% of northern heat rides one current.
Climate models say it will weaken this century.
It keeps parts of Europe 4 to 10 °C warmer.
Claims of a 15 to 20 °C crash are considered incorrect.
But winters would harden, and rain belts would shift south.
In Greenland's past, similar swings brought 8 to 15 °C within decades.
So the danger isn't an ice age. It's speed.

records.topic: What If You Took Off Your Spacesuit in Space?
records.hook: Without a spacesuit, you'd black out in 12 seconds.
records.openingLine: Without a spacesuit, you'd black out in 12 seconds.
records.secondBeat: You wouldn't explode, despite the movies.
records.scientificMechanism: in vacuum, air leaves the lungs and blood stops carrying oxygen to the brain within seconds
records.scenarioChange: an astronaut's suit lost pressure in space
records.expectedConsequence: loss of consciousness in seconds; brief exposures are survivable, long ones are fatal
records.coreQuestion: If you took off your spacesuit in space, would you explode, freeze, or suffocate?
records.misconception: You wouldn't explode or instantly freeze; oxygen loss is what kills.
visualScenes: oxygen levels dropping in bloodstream diagram
movie myth versus reality split screen
editorialTitles: What Happens If You Take Off Your Spacesuit in Space
Why Space Suffocates You Before It Freezes You

facts.claim: After 9 to 12 seconds, the deoxygenated blood reaches the brain, and it results in the loss of consciousness.
Exposure to vacuum for up to 30 seconds is unlikely to cause permanent physical damage.
Animal experiments show that rapid and complete recovery is normal for exposures shorter than 90 seconds, while longer full-body exposures are fatal and resuscitation has never been successful.
In December 1966, NASA test subject Jim LeBlanc was testing a pressurized space suit prototype in vacuum conditions.
A colleague entered the chamber within 25 seconds and gave LeBlanc oxygen.

narration.text: Without a spacesuit, you'd black out in 12 seconds.
You wouldn't explode, despite the movies.
Deoxygenated blood reaches the brain after 9 to 12 seconds.
Up to 30 seconds is unlikely to cause permanent damage.
In 1966, a NASA test subject's suit leaked in a vacuum chamber.
A colleague reached him within 25 seconds with oxygen.
Beyond 90 seconds, animal tests show resuscitation has never worked.
So space doesn't blow you up. It suffocates you fast.

records.topic: What If We Tried to Drill Through the Earth?
records.hook: Humanity's deepest hole stopped at 12,262 metres.
records.openingLine: Humanity's deepest hole stopped at 12,262 metres.
records.scientificMechanism: temperature and pressure rise with depth, softening rock and destroying drilling equipment
records.scenarioChange: engineers tried to drill toward Earth's centre
records.expectedConsequence: the drill fails in the crust, stopped by heat long before hardness becomes the limit
records.coreQuestion: If we tried to drill through the Earth, what would stop us first: rock or heat?
records.misconception: Hard rock isn't the main barrier to deep drilling; heat is.
visualScenes: Kola borehole cross-section against Earth's layers
depth comparison with Mount Everest and ocean trench
editorialTitles: What Stopped the Deepest Hole Ever Drilled
Why We Can't Drill Through the Earth

facts.claim: Drilling at Kola SG-3 began in 1970 using the Uralmash-4E, and later the Uralmash-15000 series drilling rig.
In 1974, the new Uralmash-15000 rig was installed onsite, named after the new target depth, set at 15,000 metres (49,000 ft).
The third hole reached 12,262 metres (40,230 ft) in 1989.
The drilling of the fourth hole was stopped due to higher-than-expected temperatures of 180 °C (356 °F) in 1992 at 11,882 metres (38,983 ft) of depth.
A total of five 23-centimetre-diameter (9 in) boreholes were drilled.

narration.text: Humanity's deepest hole stopped at 12,262 metres.
It barely scratched the crust.
Soviet engineers began drilling Kola SG-3 in 1970.
They aimed for 15,000 metres and fell short.
Heat stopped them: 180 °C, far above what they expected.
Rock that hot starts behaving more like plastic than stone.
Deeper down, the heat and pressure only climb.
So the planet's first defence against drilling is heat, not hardness.

records.topic: What If You Reached Absolute Zero?
records.hook: Nothing has ever reached −273.15 °C: absolute zero.
records.openingLine: Nothing has ever reached −273.15 °C: absolute zero.
records.secondBeat: The record is 38 trillionths of a degree above.
records.scientificMechanism: temperature measures particle motion; quantum mechanics leaves a minimum zero-point energy even at the limit
records.scenarioChange: matter was cooled all the way to absolute zero
records.expectedConsequence: it can be approached ever closer but never reached, and even then motion would not fully stop
records.coreQuestion: If you reached absolute zero, would everything simply stop moving?
records.misconception: Absolute zero isn't total stillness; zero-point motion remains, and the limit can't be reached.
visualScenes: ideal gas pressure line reaching zero
editorialTitles: What Happens at Absolute Zero
Why Absolute Zero Can Never Be Reached

facts.claim: The Kelvin scale is defined so that absolute zero is 0 K, equivalent to −273.15 °C on the Celsius scale, and −459.67 °F on the Fahrenheit scale.
The current world record for effective temperatures was set in 2021 at 38 picokelvin through matter-wave lensing of rubidium Bose–Einstein condensates.
In 2018, scientists at the University of Bremen achieved temperatures as low as 38 picokelvin (pK), 38 trillionths of a degree above absolute zero.
0 kelvins is defined as the point at which pressure or volume would vanish in an ideal gas.
By 1845, Michael Faraday had reached a new record for lowest temperatures by reaching −130 °C (−202 °F; 143 K).

narration.text: Nothing has ever reached −273.15 °C: absolute zero.
The record is 38 trillionths of a degree above.
It's where an ideal gas's pressure would fall to zero.
Physics lets you approach it, but never arrive.
Even there, particles would keep a minimum jiggle, called zero-point motion.
Near it, helium flows without friction and climbs container walls.
So absolute zero isn't stillness. It's a limit you chase forever.

records.topic: What If a Gamma-Ray Burst Hit Earth?
records.hook: A gamma-ray burst 8,000 light-years away could devastate Earth.
records.openingLine: A gamma-ray burst 8,000 light-years away could devastate Earth.
records.secondBeat: It wouldn't burn us. It would strip our ozone.
records.scientificMechanism: a beamed gamma-ray burst drives atmospheric chemistry that destroys ozone, letting solar ultraviolet reach the surface
records.scenarioChange: a gamma-ray burst within a few thousand light-years was beamed at Earth
records.expectedConsequence: years of ozone loss and harsh ultraviolet that hits plankton, crops and food chains
records.coreQuestion: If a gamma-ray burst hit Earth, would it burn us, or strip away our protection?
records.misconception: A distant gamma-ray burst wouldn't incinerate Earth; the damage comes through the ozone layer.
visualScenes: gamma-ray beam from a collapsing star
Milky Way map with danger radius
editorialTitles: What a Gamma-Ray Burst Would Do to Earth
Why a Gamma-Ray Burst Kills Through the Sky

facts.claim: If a GRB were to occur within the Milky Way within 5,000 to 8,000 light-years and its emission were beamed straight towards Earth, the effects could be harmful and potentially devastating for its ecosystems.
GRBs deplete ozone, with models showing a possible global reduction of 25–35%, with as much as 75% in certain locations, an effect that would last for years.
The Ordovician mass extinction 450 million years ago may have been caused by a GRB.
A GRB could potentially vaporize anything in its beams' paths within a range of around 200 light-years.

narration.text: A gamma-ray burst 8,000 light-years away could devastate Earth.
It wouldn't burn us. It would strip our ozone.
Models show a global ozone loss of 25 to 35%.
In places, losses could reach 75%, lasting for years.
Unfiltered ultraviolet light would then hit plankton and crops.
One may have triggered the Ordovician extinction, 450 million years ago.
So the deadliest light in the universe works through the sky.

records.topic: What If We Built a Space Elevator?
records.hook: A space elevator cable must stretch past 35,786 kilometres.
records.openingLine: A space elevator cable must stretch past 35,786 kilometres.
records.secondBeat: No material we can make is strong enough.
records.scientificMechanism: a tether anchored at the equator and extending past geostationary orbit is held taut by centrifugal force
records.scenarioChange: engineers built a working space elevator
records.expectedConsequence: the cable needs a breaking length far beyond steel; the bottleneck is materials science
records.coreQuestion: If we built a space elevator, what would stop it: money, or the cable itself?
records.misconception: Space elevators aren't blocked by rocket science; no cable material yet is strong enough.
visualScenes: tether rising from the equator to geostationary orbit
steel versus nanotube breaking length bars
editorialTitles: What It Would Take to Build a Space Elevator
Why Space Elevators Wait on Chemistry

facts.claim: The greatest tension on a space elevator cable is at the point of geostationary orbit, 35,786 km (22,236 mi) above the Earth's equator.
Metals like titanium, steel or aluminium alloys have breaking lengths of only 20–30 km (0.2–0.3 MPa/(kg/m3)).
A functional Earth space elevator would require a tether of 30–80 megaYuri (corresponding to 3100–8200 km of breaking length).
In 2014, Google X found that no one had yet manufactured a perfectly formed carbon nanotube strand longer than a meter.
The design's passenger climber would be able to reach the level of geosynchronous equatorial orbit (GEO) after an 8-day trip.

narration.text: A space elevator cable must stretch past 35,786 kilometres.
No material we can make is strong enough.
Steel can hang only 20 to 30 kilometres before snapping.
An Earth elevator needs 3,100 to 8,200 kilometres of breaking length.
Carbon nanotubes could work, in theory.
But no one has made a perfect strand longer than a meter.
Even then, a climber would take about 8 days to reach orbit.
So the elevator waits on chemistry, not rocket science.

records.topic: What If We Mined a Metal Asteroid?
records.hook: Psyche is the only core-like metal world we know.
records.openingLine: Psyche is the only core-like metal world we know.
records.secondBeat: It's about 278 kilometres across at its longest.
records.scientificMechanism: a body's bulk density reveals its mix of metal, rock and empty space before anyone lands on it
records.scenarioChange: humans tried to mine the metal-rich asteroid Psyche
records.expectedConsequence: the first obstacle is knowing what it is made of; hauling metal across the Solar System comes after
records.coreQuestion: If we mined a metal asteroid, would it be solid treasure or a rubble pile?
records.misconception: Psyche probably isn't a solid ball of iron; its density is about half that of pure iron-nickel.
visualScenes: density comparison bars with iron meteorites
trajectory from Earth to the asteroid belt
editorialTitles: What If We Mined the Metal Asteroid Psyche
Why Psyche May Not Be Solid Metal

facts.claim: Psyche has a shape consistent with a Jacobi ellipsoid and dimensions within a few km of 278 km x 238 km x 171 km.
Psyche has a bulk density of 3.977±0.253 g/cm3, considerably higher than most small Solar System bodies.
The iron-nickel found in most iron meteorites has a bulk density of 7.9 g/cm3.
The Psyche spacecraft was launched on 13 October 2023, with an expected arrival in 2029.
16 Psyche is the only metallic core-like body discovered so far.

narration.text: Psyche is the only core-like metal world we know.
It's about 278 kilometres across at its longest.
Its density is around 4 grams per cubic centimetre.
Pure iron-nickel would be nearly double that, at 7.9.
So Psyche is likely metal mixed with rock or rubble.
NASA's probe launched in 2023 and should arrive in 2029.
Mining it would mean hauling metal across hundreds of millions of kilometres.
So first we have to learn what it's actually made of.

records.topic: What If the Tunguska Blast Happened Over a City?
records.hook: A 50-metre rock flattened 2,150 square kilometres of forest.
records.openingLine: A 50-metre rock flattened 2,150 square kilometres of forest.
records.secondBeat: It exploded in mid-air, leaving no crater.
records.scientificMechanism: a stony asteroid that explodes in the air releases its energy as a shockwave rather than a crater
records.scenarioChange: a Tunguska-size airburst occurred over a major city
records.expectedConsequence: widespread structural damage across an area the size of a metropolis, without any crater
records.coreQuestion: If the Tunguska blast happened over a city today, what would do the damage: impact or shockwave?
records.misconception: Tunguska left no crater; the object exploded in the air.
visualScenes: Siberian forest flattened in radial pattern
2,150 km² footprint over a city map
standing scorched trees at the centre
editorialTitles: What If Tunguska Exploded Over a City
Why Tunguska Left No Crater

facts.claim: The event is attributed to a meteor air burst, the atmospheric explosion of a stony asteroid about 50–60 m (160–200 ft) wide.
Occurring over an area of 2,150 km2 (830 sq mi) in the sparsely populated East Siberian taiga, the explosion felled a significant amount of trees.
The object is thought to have exploded at an altitude of 5–10 km (3–6 mi) rather than hitting the Earth's surface, leaving no impact crater.
Estimates of its energy have ranged from 3–30 megatons of TNT (13–126 PJ).
Investigators found a zone, roughly 8 km (5.0 mi) across, where the trees were scorched and devoid of branches, but still standing upright.

narration.text: A 50-metre rock flattened 2,150 square kilometres of forest.
It exploded in mid-air, leaving no crater.
The blast came 5 to 10 kilometres above Siberia.
Estimates put its energy at 3 to 30 megatons.
Over a city, windows and roofs would fail across that whole area.
Right below the blast, trees stayed upright but were stripped bare.
So the danger isn't the impact. It's the shockwave from above.

records.topic: What If Earth Became Like Venus?
records.hook: Earth's near-twin Venus has a 462 °C surface.
records.openingLine: Earth's near-twin Venus has a 462 °C surface.
records.secondBeat: That's hotter than Mercury, which is closer to the Sun.
records.scientificMechanism: a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps outgoing heat through the greenhouse effect
records.scenarioChange: Earth's carbon ended up in its atmosphere, as on Venus
records.expectedConsequence: a crushing, scorching surface; the difference between the twins is where their carbon is stored
records.coreQuestion: If Earth became like Venus, what would it take, and what would change first?
records.misconception: Venus isn't hottest because it's closest to the Sun; its atmosphere is the reason.
visualScenes: Earth and Venus side by side to scale
carbon stored in Earth's rocks and oceans
editorialTitles: What If Earth Became Like Venus
Why Venus Is Hotter Than Mercury

facts.claim: Venus has a diameter of 12,103.6 km, only 638.4 km less than Earth's, and its mass is 81.5% of Earth's.
Venus's dense atmosphere is 96.5% carbon dioxide, causing an intense greenhouse effect, with most of the remaining 3.5% being nitrogen.
The CO2-rich atmosphere generates the strongest greenhouse effect in the Solar System, creating surface temperatures of at least 735 K (462 °C; 864 °F).
The density at the surface is 65 kg/m3, 6.5% that of water or 50 times as dense as Earth's atmosphere at 293 K (20 °C; 68 °F) at sea level.

narration.text: Earth's near-twin Venus has a 462 °C surface.
That's hotter than Mercury, which is closer to the Sun.
Venus has 81.5% of Earth's mass.
But its atmosphere is 96.5% carbon dioxide.
That traps heat in the strongest greenhouse effect in the Solar System.
Its air at the surface is 50 times denser than ours.
Earth's carbon is mostly locked in rocks and oceans instead.
So the difference between the twins is where the carbon lives.

records.topic: What If You Stopped Sleeping Entirely?
records.hook: After 24 hours awake, your brain starts failing you.
records.openingLine: After 24 hours awake, your brain starts failing you.
records.secondBeat: The record is 264 hours: 11 days awake.
records.scientificMechanism: sleep pressure builds with time awake until the brain forces brief microsleeps
records.scenarioChange: a person tried to stop sleeping entirely
records.expectedConsequence: attention and reaction times collapse within a day, and the brain begins taking sleep involuntarily
records.coreQuestion: If you stopped sleeping entirely, how long before your brain took it anyway?
records.misconception: You can't simply push through; the brain slips into microsleeps whether you want them or not.
editorialTitles: What Happens If You Stop Sleeping
Why Your Brain Takes Sleep Anyway

facts.claim: Gardner stayed awake for 264 hours (11 days), breaking the previous record of 260 hours held by Tom Rounds of Honolulu.
The US National Sleep Foundation recommends that adults aim for 7 hours of sleep per night.
A study in 2025 found that just after 24 hours of sleep deprivation, healthy participants showed significant decreases in attentional processing and increased reaction times.
Microsleeps usually last for a few seconds, usually no longer than 15 seconds, and happen most frequently when a person is trying to stay awake when they are feeling sleepy.

In a study that followed over 160,000 healthy, non-obese adults, those who self-reported sleep duration less than six hours a day were at increased risk for developing multiple cardiometabolic risk factors.

narration.text: After 24 hours awake, your brain starts failing you.
The record is 264 hours: 11 days awake.
Attention drops and reaction times slow.
Tired brains slip into microsleeps, usually under 15 seconds.
You can't choose them. They strike while you try to stay awake.
Adults are advised to aim for 7 hours a night.
Short sleep is linked to higher cardiometabolic risk.
